# Running One Complete Study {#sec-running-the-loop}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"In theory, there is no difference between theory and practice. But, in practice, there is."*
>
> — widely circulated aphorism
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** The aphorism fits this study, which compares a model proposal against a fixed aspect-ratio heuristic in an architecture simulator. The model's explanation fails a declared distinguishing contrast. It is useful because the recorded results are less exciting than the initial hypothesis.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
How does a 3\ W XR system goal become one tool-evaluable architecture
decision, and what can that local study establish when the model ties a simple
heuristic and its explanation fails?
:::

The Lighthouse asks for a low-power, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for
a real-time mobile XR workload. A useful answer has to connect workload
behavior, compiler and runtime support, memory traffic, accelerator choices,
verification, a 3\ W subsystem budget, thermal behavior, and physical
implementation. This chapter does not pretend that one retained simulator run
answers all of those questions. It traces the full-system goal down to one
local array-shape decision, shows exactly what happened when that decision was
run, and then returns the limited result to the XR system.

The recorded numbers come from one model runtime and SCALE-Sim, an analytical
systolic-array simulator. The local architecture outcome is no change under
the declared rule, the model and fixed heuristic arms tie, and the model's
directional prediction fails its predeclared test. The architecture action
remains pending, and the record does not name the accountable owner. A study
that keeps these inconvenient outcomes visible shows more about engineering
practice than a cleaner success story would.

The run guards against changing the comparison after seeing the result.
Simulators expose many configurable choices, and model outputs can
change with phrasing. A study can therefore make a candidate look stronger by
retuning simulator settings, weakening its baseline, or silently discarding
unsuccessful model prompts. These post-result choices are the same kind that
produced overoptimistic, irreproducible results across hundreds of
machine-learning studies [@KapoorNarayanan2023Leakage].

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The shifting baseline"}
**The trap.** A design team celebrated a 20% architectural speedup from a novel accelerator proposal, only to discover weeks later that the baseline software was accidentally compiled without standard optimization flags (`-O3`). When the baseline was properly optimized, the entire architectural gain vanished.

**The lesson.** Unfixed baselines create illusions of progress. If the baseline is allowed to shift or remain untuned during an architectural study, any measured "improvement" is meaningless. This scenario is a composite of a recurring pattern in architecture evaluations, not a single documented incident.
:::

In a real EDA environment, the penalty for guessing wrong can be large.
Waiting hours for a physical routing failure consumes far more calendar time
and limited tool licenses than waiting for a Python syntax error. This
retained run is inexpensive, but its fixed budget and stopping rule show how
those costs would have to enter a more consequential study.

Before any model or simulator output is known, the architect fixes the
workload, legal array shapes, simulator configuration, comparison budget,
rejection criteria, and decision boundary. Fixing these choices prevents
post-result goalpost moving. It enforces discipline without claiming the
choices were intrinsically optimal. The fixed aspect-ratio heuristic is the
comparison arm that the model-based generator must beat
(@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization). This record should also
have named the accountable owner for the pending action, but it did not.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Trace a full-system XR goal to one tool-evaluable architecture decision and
  state which workload, software, memory, verification, power, thermal, and
  physical questions remain outside the run.
- Preregister the workload, legal candidates, score, decision margin, and
  evaluation budget before any candidate is measured.
- Reconstruct the actual execution sequence, including setup failure, repair,
  model call, simulator evaluations, missing cost fields, and retained
  provenance.
- Report the architecture outcome, AI contribution, mechanism explanation, and
  stopping decision as four separate judgments.
- Distinguish replay of the retained computation from an independent
  architecture check and identify the stronger comparison required before a
  broader method claim.

:::

## From the XR Moonshot to One Architecture Decision

The study below applies the book's method to one concrete architecture problem.
It uses three synthetic general matrix multiplication (GEMM) layers as
XR-motivated stand-ins for a localized accelerator question within the
Lighthouse prompt from @sec-moonshot. They are not traces derived from an
identified spatial-tracking pipeline, XR application, or deployed product.
The system goal remains a 3\ W, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for a
real-time mobile XR platform.

That system goal creates several coupled architecture questions:

- **Workload:** Which XR operators, inputs, phases, deadlines, and tail-latency
  limits must the subsystem support?
- **Software:** How will compilers, runtimes, libraries, mappings, and the
  RISC-V interface expose the accelerator?
- **Memory:** How much traffic reaches local SRAM and shared memory, and how
  does it contend with host cores, sensors, and the display path?
- **Accelerator:** Which array shape, dataflow, precision, buffering, and
  control choices belong in the candidate subsystem?
- **Verification:** Which functional, performance, security, and interface
  properties must be checked, and at what implementation depth?
- **Power and thermal behavior:** Does the complete subsystem remain inside
  the 3\ W target across the operating conditions that matter?
- **Physical implementation:** Can the candidate close timing, route, deliver
  power, and fit the selected process, voltage, temperature, package, and area
  constraints?

The retained study can answer only one local question inside the accelerator
item. It compares several systolic-array shapes under one fixed analytical
model and synthetic workload slice. It does not execute the compiler, runtime,
host-memory system, RTL, formal checks, synthesis, place and route, power
delivery, thermal model, or a real XR workload.

This is a separate executed array-shape study, not the prospective cache study
used elsewhere in the book. Its purpose is to follow one decision through
declared inputs, candidate selection, execution, interpretation, and stopping
using retained artifacts.

The prospective cache study, `XR-L2-CAP-A`, stops at a ready-to-run plan. The
book does not have a retained cache implementation and measurement path that
could execute that plan, so it does not invent an outcome. Its recorded status
is *not run*, and its choice among the 2, 3, and 4\ MB candidates remains open.
That is an honest stop under the lifecycle in @sec-architecture-20-ontology,
not a recommendation. The array-shape study is used here because its inputs,
tool path, and raw results can be retained and inspected.

The study fixes one local decision, a 32 by 32 baseline, fifteen legal array
shapes, a one-percent change margin, equal simulator-call budgets for two
proposal arms, and conditions that stop the run. Only the two array dimensions
may change. The rest of the accelerator, the host system, implementation, and
product commitment remain outside the study
(@sec-architecture-20-ontology).

The explicit design state is small enough to inspect directly. It contains the
workload matrices, legal dimension set, processing-element limit, fixed
dataflow and simulator configuration, mutable height and width fields,
proposal history, and known blind spots. The workload is synthetic, the score
omits memory traffic, and no energy or physical-design model is active. Those
absences remain part of the state rather than being filled by general model
knowledge (@sec-data-representations-world-models).

Candidate selection gives one model a generation role and uses one fixed
aspect-ratio heuristic as the comparison arm. Neither arm predicts simulator
outcomes or chooses an adaptive sequence of evaluations. Both submit three
nonbaseline shapes plus the shared baseline under equal simulator-call
budgets. The heuristic is intentionally simple, so a tie can show only that
the model failed to beat this comparator. It cannot establish parity with a
competent human architecture study or with the strongest practical
conventional search
(@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization).

Each candidate is bound to a retained model call, schema, SCALE-Sim
configuration, input and report hashes, and typed execution status. The record
also exposes what it failed to retain, including the rejected schema artifacts
and an exact prompt copy matching the recorded hash
(@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces). Candidate scores are
compared under one frozen simulator, and a separate matched contrast tests the
model's directional explanation. Replay can recheck the calculation but
remains inside the same workload, simulator, score, and assumptions
(@sec-feedback-verification-trust).

This intake reveals the chapter's limits before the first result appears. The
run uses a different local target from the prospective cache study, one
recorded model call, a weak heuristic, a narrow analytical simulator, no
complete accounting of human effort, and no materially different architecture
check. It can show how one configured subset of the proposed design system
behaves in one local run. It cannot establish the Lighthouse moonshot or the
general value of AI-assisted design.

To make the problem computationally tractable, the study narrows the top-level
system intent from the full SoC to this synthetic workload slice. The slice
does not claim to have been extracted from a real spatial-tracking
implementation. It provides a way to map a system constraint into one local
architecture question without claiming that the local result represents the
complete system.

Instead of evaluating every geometry, the generator proposes candidates that
must clear declared rejection checks before simulation. In a production study
those checks could include die area and wiring congestion. This run checks
schema validity, the legal dimension set, and a processing-element cap.

One recorded model call proposes three legal systolic-array datapath shapes for
a compact three-layer matrix-multiplication workload. A fixed
aspect-ratio heuristic proposes three shapes under the same four-call simulator
budget. SCALE-Sim 3.0.0 evaluates both arms[^fn-study-arm-c08] under one frozen
configuration [@RajEtAl2025ScaleSimV3], and a declared workload contrast then
tests the model's mechanism prediction. The study excludes model benchmarking,
full-chip XR evaluation, and tapeout. It asks whether a no-change architecture
outcome, an equal-call tie, and an unsupported mechanism explanation can be
reported without being recast as an AI success. SCALE-Sim computes cycle
counts, layer utilization, and modeled memory traffic from an analytical
dataflow model. It performs no timing closure or physical design, and this run
enabled no energy model.

[^fn-study-arm-c08]: **Arm**: In experimental design, one of the parallel groups in a controlled comparison, as in the treatment and control arms of a clinical trial. The model and the fixed heuristic are this study's two proposal arms.

Array shape is a real architecture choice. Google's first TPU used a 256 by
256 weight-stationary[^fn-weight-stationary-c08] systolic array
[@JouppiEtAl2017TPU], while TPU v4 uses 128 by 128 matrix units
[@JouppiEtAl2023TPUv4]. The change across generations does not by itself
establish why either geometry was chosen, but it shows that one family did not
treat array shape as a universal constant. The 32 by 32 baseline here is a
fixed reference point rather than a claim of global optimality among all
fifteen legal shapes. Another reader can inspect the proposal and rerun the
recorded simulator computation without mistaking that replay for independent
validation of the workload, score, or simulator.

[^fn-weight-stationary-c08]: **Weight-stationary dataflow**: A mapping in which each processing element holds one weight in place while activations stream past it and partial sums accumulate across the array. Keeping the weights still removes their memory traffic from the inner loop, which is why the array's shape rather than its raw size decides how much of it stays busy on a given layer.

Most of this procedure is familiar architecture work where an architect
defines the comparison, validates tool inputs, evaluates candidates, tests an
explanation, and decides whether the evidence warrants a change. AI
participation adds a proposal and explanation whose scope, output, budget,
provenance, and authority must be controlled. This integration neither changes
what SCALE-Sim computed nor grants the model authority to decide what happens
next.

## What This Study Can and Cannot See {#sec-executed-scale-study}

The retained tool path can observe legal array dimensions, SCALE-Sim status,
cycles, average layer utilization, and modeled memory traffic for the three
synthetic XR-motivated GEMMs. It can compare the evaluated candidates under a
common dataflow, scratchpad capacity, interface width, simulator version, and
local score. It cannot observe whether a real XR pipeline is represented,
whether the software can use the candidate efficiently, whether shared-memory
traffic violates a system limit, or whether the design closes timing, area,
power, thermal, reliability, or physical checks.

Preregistration fixes the terms of that limited view before any candidate is
measured. The decision question, the judgments the record must support, and the
constraints and budgets that define the run are declared first, so no later
result can quietly redefine what would have counted as success. The
declarations that follow make the simulator numbers reviewable without making
the simulator a model of the complete XR subsystem.

### Defining the Decision

The architecture question is deliberately narrow to test a precise hypothesis without overextending the methodology.

> Under the declared local rule, does any candidate selected by the recorded
> model or fixed aspect-ratio heuristic warrant follow-up over the 32 by 32
> baseline, and does the model's directional prediction survive its declared
> contrast?

A 32 by 32 matrix unit was selected before execution as a compact, square
reference, not on a claim of optimality. The architect also held a prior that
elongated shapes could cost wire length, an axis this simulator does not
measure. The fixed aspect-ratio rule is a simple and weak proposer. A tie
against it shows only that the model did not beat that rule under the equal
simulator-call budget. It says nothing about how either would compare with a
competent human architecture study.

The workload contains three synthetic GEMM[^fn-gemm-c08] layers used as an
XR-like stand-in. It is not a trace from a spatial-tracking pipeline or a
complete XR application. Their (M, N, K) dimensions are 128 by 128 by 256, 64
by 192 by 128, and 32 by 128 by 192. The mechanism test exchanges M and N in
the two nonsquare layers. Recording these dimensions lets a later reader
recompute the tie and inspect the aspect-ratio rule, though it cannot make the
slice representative.

Only the datapath's array dimensions vary. Dataflow, on-chip scratchpad
capacity, interface bandwidth, layout, simulator version, workload, deadline,
and scoring rule remain fixed. This narrowness isolates array shape within the
declared model, but the preregistration omitted a resolving-power check. After
proposal generation, the two arms differed by only one nonbaseline candidate
each. The completed comparison can report that weak discrimination; it cannot
claim that the tie was inevitable before the proposals were seen.

[^fn-gemm-c08]: **GEMM (general matrix multiply)**: The dense matrix-matrix multiplication kernel, conventionally described by the three dimensions M, N, and K, that accounts for most of the arithmetic in a neural-network layer. An accelerator array is ultimately judged by how well its height and width fit the M, N, and K of the layers it has to run, which is why those numbers, not the layer names, are what a shape study must record.

### The Four Judgments

A candidate ranking does not answer every question in an AI-assisted architecture study, so this experiment produces four distinct judgments from different parts of the record.

- **Architecture outcome.** Does any evaluated nonbaseline shape clear the local decision margin over 32 by 32?
- **AI contribution.** Does the recorded model arm find a better score than the fixed aspect-ratio heuristic under the same simulator-call budget?
- **Mechanism explanation.** Does the model's directional prediction survive its declared distinguishing contrast?[^fn-planned-contrast-c08]
- **Stopping decision.** Is another evaluation warranted under the predeclared rule and current project scope?

[^fn-planned-contrast-c08]: **Contrast**: In the design of experiments, a specific comparison between conditions planned before the data are seen. The M/N-transposed workload is this study's planned comparison for testing the model's directional explanation.

These judgments can disagree. A model might propose a competitive candidate
without beating the heuristic. A useful candidate might arrive with a failed
explanation, and a study can stop even though most of the legal design space
remains unevaluated. The executed comparison below reports all four outcomes
without combining them into a single claim that the model or the complete
discipline succeeded.

### Separating Outcomes From Claims

The preregistration keeps the architecture-outcome and AI-contribution claims
separate. This deliberate decoupling enforces one rule. The generator proposes
candidates, and a separate simulator computes the declared quantities under
its stated model. The model does not grade its own proposal, and the
simulator does not become ground truth merely because it is deterministic. A
schema-valid model response is therefore not an architecture result. The study
runs from a frozen plan through candidate selection, execution, interpretation,
and four separate judgments (@fig-bounded-study-workflow).

![**One record supports four different judgments.** The plan is frozen before candidate selection, execution, and interpretation. Only after those stages does the architect read the architecture outcome, study-local AI contribution, mechanism status, and stopping result separately.](images/ch8_design_loop_workflow){#fig-bounded-study-workflow width="100%" fig-alt="Workflow diagram of an architecture study. Four stages run left to right: freeze plan, select candidates, execute and record, and interpret the record. The last stage feeds four separate judgments: architecture outcome, AI contribution, mechanism status, and stopping."}

Read the upper row from the frozen plan through candidate selection and
recorded execution to interpretation. Only the interpreted record feeds the
four boxes below. Those branches keep the architecture outcome, study-local AI
contribution, mechanism status, and stopping decision from substituting for one
another. The final box stops this local study while leaving the architecture
action pending, so completing the workflow does not itself authorize a design
change.

- **Architecture-outcome claim.** At least one evaluated nonbaseline shape
selected by either arm improves the local decision score over the 32 by 32
baseline by at least 1 percent for the frozen workload and simulator
configuration. The outcome is no change if none of those evaluated shapes
clears that decision margin.

- **AI-contribution claim.** With four SCALE-Sim evaluations per arm, including
the same mandatory baseline, the recorded model arm finds a score at least 1
percent lower than the fixed aspect-ratio heuristic arm. A difference within 1
percent is a tie. A worse model result is adverse. Equal simulator calls do not
equalize model inference, human setup, prior knowledge encoded in the heuristic,
or total labor. One model call cannot establish a population-level result about
a model family, even if it wins.

These two outcome claims were fixed before proposal generation. The mechanism
hypothesis follows a different sequence. The architect fixed a mirrored-shape
test on the original and M/N-transposed workloads, then required the model to
supply its directional prediction before any simulation.

The local score is

$$
S = \frac{\text{total cycles}}
         {\text{average layer utilization}/100},
$$

with lower values preferred. This composite is not a true Area-Delay Product
(ADP). For $L$ layers with work $W_i$, cycles $C_i$, and the implemented
unweighted average of per-layer utilization, the approximation
$u_i \approx W_i/(\text{PE}\,C_i)$ gives

$$
S \approx
\frac{\text{PE}\,L\sum_i C_i}
     {\sum_i W_i/C_i}.
$$

Only for a single layer, or under uniform scaling across layers, does this
reduce to a squared dependence on cycles. The study therefore treats the score
as a predeclared local ordering rule, not as ADP, a universal accelerator
metric, or a physical measurement. The 1,024-processing-element legality cap,
not the score, forecloses oversized arrays. Reporting cycles and utilization
separately exposes the ingredients the score combines, though neither reveals
an omitted axis such as memory traffic.

The retained runner defines total cycles as the sum of the `Total Cycles`
column in SCALE-Sim's `COMPUTE_REPORT.csv`. It excludes the separate `Total
Cycles (incl. prefetch)` column. The frozen preregistration says only "total
cycles," so the executable runner, rather than the preregistration prose,
supplies this distinction. Including prefetch would change the baseline and 16
by 64 counts to 17,371 and 17,500. Their 0.742 percent difference would remain
inside the 1 percent tie margin, so none of the four judgments would change.

A fair comparison requires the evaluation budget, workload, simulator settings,
rejection criteria, and decision boundary to be frozen before either arm
produces results. The frozen rules keep the two proposal arms comparable and
make later changes visible (@tbl-executed-study-protocol).

| **Element** | **Frozen rule** |
| --- | --- |
| **Workloads** | One three-layer GEMM slice, plus a versioned copy with M and N exchanged for the mechanism test. |
| **Legal shapes** | Rows and columns each in {8, 16, 32, 64, 128}; product no greater than 1,024 processing elements. These rules admit fifteen shapes. The cap is a declared scope bound for this study, chosen to keep candidates in a range plausible for a 3\ W mobile subsystem, not a limit derived from the power budget by this simulator, which was run here with no power or area model enabled. |
| **Environment** | SCALE-Sim 3.0.0, GEMM interface, weight-stationary dataflow [@ChenEtAl2016Eyeriss], 128 KiB per SRAM, and 64 interface words per cycle. |
| **Baseline and rejection criteria** | Insert 32 by 32 into both arms; reject shapes above 1,024 processing elements or runs above 90,000 cycles. |
| **Proposal arms** | Three model proposals and three candidates from a fixed aggregate-aspect-ratio heuristic. |
| **Evaluation budget** | Four SCALE-Sim evaluations per arm, including the mandatory 32 by 32 baseline; no post-result replacement. |
| **Model repair** | At most one complete repair response after reported schema or legality errors; invalid proposals consume the initial call. |
| **Decision margin** | At least 1 percent on the lower-is-better local score; differences inside the margin are ties. |
| **Mechanism probe** | Four shared runs comparing 16 by 64 and 64 by 16 on the original and M/N-transposed workloads. |
| **Decision boundary** | The recorded result may motivate a clearly scoped follow-up experiment or stopping. It cannot authorize RTL, tapeout, or a system intent decision. |

: **The comparison was fixed before evaluation.** Both proposal arms use the same workload, SCALE-Sim configuration, rejection criteria, baseline, and four-evaluation budget. {#tbl-executed-study-protocol tbl-colwidths="[22,68]"}

The workload, legal shapes, environment, and rejection criteria fix the
architecture comparison. The proposal and evaluation budgets prevent either
arm from receiving extra candidates after results appear. Because this study
meters one analytical stage, the budget row can record a flat four simulator
calls per arm. The repair and decision rules fix how invalid model output and
small score differences will be treated. The mechanism contrast challenges the
generated explanation, while the final row leaves approval outside both the
model and simulator.

A production physical-design flow needs a different cost budget. Its stages
can vary by orders of magnitude in runtime, compute, and license use, so raw
call count represents their cost poorly. Such a flow might meter CPU-hours and
license-hours, then screen weak candidates with floorplan estimates before
paying for detailed routing.

Predeclaring these choices forces any change to the candidate, metric, or stopping rule out into the open, where it can be checked against the record instead of silently validating a flawed candidate.

Preregistration does not outlaw exploration. It separates exploratory work
from the confirmatory run whose results feed the study outcome
[@NosekEtAl2018Preregistration]. Any run used to choose a frozen study choice
must remain exploratory and cannot also count as confirmatory evidence. Those
choices include the workload, candidate space, prompt, baseline, simulator
configuration, score, threshold, budget, contrast, and rejection criteria. This
protocol did not record prompt-development iterations or author hours before
the freeze, so total human effort remains unknown. A future protocol should add
those fields before work begins rather than claim that this frozen record
contained them.

Nor does preregistration intrinsically justify the
three-layer workload, local score, 32 by 32 baseline, 1 percent decision margin,
90,000-cycle cutoff, SCALE-Sim abstraction, or four-call budget. Each remains
an architecture choice that would need a rationale and sensitivity analysis
before a broader decision relied on it.

The 1 percent margin is a local decision threshold over deterministic
SCALE-Sim outputs, not a statement that those outputs are within 1 percent of
silicon. Running both arms through the same frozen model removes configuration
drift and may cancel some shared error, but candidate-dependent modeling error
need not cancel. This study did not estimate that residual error. The margin
therefore resolves only the comparison as represented by this simulator,
workload, and score.

Every rule frozen in @tbl-executed-study-protocol exists because a comparison left unfixed can be adjusted after the result arrives, and nothing in the published record will show that it was. An entire research literature demonstrates the consequence at scale.

::: {.callout-war-story title="Civil-war prediction and the margin that was a leak"}
**The claim.** Political-science studies reported that complex machine-learning
models substantially outperformed logistic regression at predicting the onset
of civil war.

**The gap.** The results did not reproduce after researchers removed leakage
between training and test data, often caused by filling in missing values before
the split [@KapoorNarayanan2023Leakage]. After correction, the complex models
did not beat logistic regression in the examined cases. The survey found
related leakage across 17 fields.

**The lesson.** Preregistration blocks post-result retuning and reselection, but
it can also freeze a flawed data pipeline. A credible study therefore fixes the
comparison before execution and separately audits the pipeline that produces
the result.
:::

## Choosing Candidates Under a Fixed Budget

The candidate-selection comparison has two recorded arms. A generator may
return three nonbaseline shapes, while a fixed aggregate-aspect-ratio rule
selects three nonbaseline shapes from the same legal set. Both arms also
include the 32 by 32 baseline and receive four SCALE-Sim calls. The heuristic
is intentionally simple. A tie can show only that the recorded model proposal
did not beat that rule under this simulator-call budget. It cannot establish
parity with an expert architect, exhaustive enumeration, a solver, or the
strongest conventional search.

The legal space contains only fifteen shapes, but the frozen run evaluated
five unique shapes. No exhaustive, solver-based, or expert diagnostic was run.
One of those comparisons is required before the chapter can make a broader
method claim. It remains follow-up work and cannot be treated as retroactive
evidence for the frozen comparison.

The heuristic rule and its declared candidates belong to the
preregistration. Its executable implementation lives in repository code, but
the retained manifest does not bind that implementation to a specific commit.
The record can therefore show the declared comparison and the outputs that
were retained without proving the exact historical code identity from the
manifest alone.

### The Mechanism Hypothesis

As established in @sec-data-representations-world-models, general knowledge is
insufficient without explicit project constraints. The representation for this
study is small, describing one accelerator under one set of fixed conditions
rather than the accelerator in general. The fifteen legal shapes, baseline,
mutable array dimensions, fixed simulator conditions, local score, and
workload matrices form the explicit design state. Formalizing these variables
keeps authority over the design boundaries with the architect. In this
instance, the candidate representation changes only the datapath's
`ArrayHeight` and `ArrayWidth`, while the weight-stationary dataflow
[@ChenEtAl2016Eyeriss], SRAM capacity, interface bandwidth, layout, workload,
and simulator version remain fixed.

That representation is useful only if a candidate change can be connected to a predicted consequence. The model proposed three shape changes and predicted that a wider 16 by 64 array would better match the workload's N dimensions than its mirrored 64 by 16 alternative. It further predicted that exchanging M and N in the workload would reverse the winner. A fluent rationale can misstate the cause of a proposal [@TurpinEtAl2023Unfaithful], so the study records this statement as a hypothesis to test rather than as evidence.

### Fixing Environment and Roles

The roles are fixed before execution. The model and fixed heuristic select
candidates, but neither produces the local score or approves an architecture
change. Validation scripts may reject malformed or illegal output without
deciding whether the workload or objective is appropriate. SCALE-Sim
calculates cycles, utilization, and modeled memory traffic. The retained runner
derives the local score and result status from those outputs. Neither
calculation establishes simulator fidelity. The architect interprets the four
judgments. The technical record retains the pending status, but it does not
identify a named accountable owner; author confirmation remains pending.

That omission cannot be repaired by silently assigning an owner after the
results are known. The historical record can support a technical
recommendation, but it cannot show who had authority to accept it when the
study ran. Any later assignment must be recorded as a post-study action with
the assignee, date, local authority, artifact received, and conditions for
reopening or escalation. Until that happens, the study can close technically
while the architecture action remains unowned and pending.

## What Happened When Runs Began

With the roles and constraints fixed, the architect invokes the model. The
retained study record says the model received the architecture question, legal
dimension set, processing-element budget, workload matrix dimensions, fixed
environment assumptions, mandatory baseline, output schema, scoring
definition, and limits on what the result could support, but not the fixed
heuristic's candidates or
simulator results. The surviving prompt is consistent with that intended
context, but its hash does not match the frozen record, so the package cannot
independently verify the exact context supplied to the recorded call. The
retained response proposes a design mutation by naming three candidates,
predicting qualitative behavior, stating an anticipated failure mode, and
offering a directional mechanism with a testable failure condition. The
architect evaluates this output as a candidate, not a final decision.

The actual chronology contains one setup failure and no candidate failure. The
response-format service rejected the first schema before inference, the schema
was amended, one valid model call returned three legal candidates, and no model
repair call followed. The runner then recorded all twelve simulator
evaluations as successful. The record reports no simulator timeout, candidate
retry, or failed evaluation, and it gives no per-evaluation timestamp or
complete human-effort account. Those absences matter because a clean result
table alone would hide which recovery behavior was exercised and which was
never tested.

### Handling Toolchain Errors

The first attempt to invoke the runtime never reached inference. The
response-format service rejected the request's JSON Schema before any tokens
were generated.[^fn-json-schema-c08] This was an invalid request caused by the
study setup, not a model result and not evidence about an architecture
candidate. The schema-only correction was recorded before inference.

[^fn-json-schema-c08]: **JSON Schema rejection (detail)**: The record states that two constant-string properties lacked explicit types, so no model output or usage was produced. The preregistration amendment preserves the old and new schema hashes but not the rejected schema body or service response, so the exact failure cannot be independently inspected from this package.

Fixing the schema was a recorded setup repair, not a concession to the model
or a change to the architecture comparison. A harness driving a real toolchain
would need to distinguish setup defects, transient service failures,
deterministic tool failures, and candidate violations from the available
records. Repeating an unchanged input can help diagnose a failure, but
repetition alone does not reveal its cause. A deterministic wrapper defect can
repeat without saying anything about the candidate, while a candidate can
trigger an intermittent resource failure. Only a failure linked to a named
candidate property should become negative architecture evidence. This run
recorded only the pre-inference schema rejection, which carried no
architectural information.

Correctly classifying the retained failures is only half the accounting. A run
that discards failed attempts before writing anything down leaves no way to
reconstruct the cost of reaching its reported result.

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The illusion of zero-shot success"}
**The trap.** An AI model generates a highly optimized architecture design on the first try, and the write-up presents the result as zero-shot capability, a first-try success with no examples or iteration.

**The mechanism.** The write-up omits the dozens of prior manual iterations in which an architect tweaked the prompt, added constraints, and fixed syntax errors. This prompt shopping hides the true human-in-the-loop cost, framing a heavily curated result as autonomous intelligence. The case here is a composite of a pattern reviewers report across AI-for-design evaluations, not one specific publication.

**The lesson.** A credible record includes all inference attempts, repairs, and
environment failures. The true cost of a candidate includes the discarded
prompts and failed runs that led to it.
:::

### Capturing Call Provenance

The subsequent call returned a schema-valid response. Since semantic validation found three unique legal candidates, no repair call was made. The complete response is retained, not only the candidate coordinates or a prose summary. The runtime exposed only part of the provenance needed to identify the call. The available fields bound how far its identity can be reconstructed, and missing values remain unavailable rather than inferred (@tbl-model-provenance). A production EDA run would fill the execution-environment field far more heavily, pinning the PDK version, standard-cell library PVT corners,[^fn-pvt-corners-c08] binary patches, and Tcl setup scripts through Nix or containers to prevent environmental drift; this study carried none of that toolchain, so the field is recorded as empty rather than left to inference.

| **Provenance field** | **Recorded value** |
| --- | --- |
| **Provider and interface** | OpenAI through Codex CLI 0.144.4, noninteractive ephemeral execution, read-only empty workspace. |
| **Execution environment** | None beyond the runtime above; the study ran in a read-only empty workspace with no EDA toolchain, PDK, or standard-cell libraries in play. |
| **Requested and accepted model alias** | gpt-5.4; provider revision or digest was not exposed. |
| **Time** | 2026-07-14 18:21:51--18:22:24 UTC; 32.90 seconds wall time. |
| **Settings** | Medium reasoning effort; temperature, top-p, and seed were not exposed or available through the runtime. |
| **Usage** | 13,223 input tokens, including 1,920 cached; 1,446 output tokens, including 516 reasoning tokens. |
| **Cost** | Currency cost was not reported, so none is inferred. |
| **Interaction** | One valid proposal call, no repair call, and no observed tool calls. Schema, output, and provenance hashes are recorded. The retained prompt does not match its recorded hash. |
| **Privacy** | No credential, session identifier, or private configuration is stored. |

: **Provenance is only as good as the runtime exposes.** The record reports the values the runtime supplied and marks the rest as unavailable rather than inferring them. {#tbl-model-provenance tbl-colwidths="[27,63]"}

Read down from the provider, interface, and execution environment to the model
alias, time, and exposed settings, then to usage, cost, interaction history,
and privacy. The decisive pattern is the boundary around what the runtime did
not expose. Provider revision, sampling settings, seed, and currency cost are
not reconstructed from the retained response. The table identifies the
recorded call as far as the available fields allow, but it cannot make the
hosted generator exactly reproducible.

Temperature and top-p control how broadly a language model samples among
plausible next tokens. A seed aids repeatability only when the provider, exact
model revision, and sampling implementation are also fixed. Provider-reported
input, output, cached, and reasoning tokens are accounting fields for that
runtime, not comparable units of engineering work across different models.

[^fn-pvt-corners-c08]: **PVT corners**: The process, voltage, and temperature extremes that a standard-cell library is characterized at, such as a slow-process, low-voltage, high-temperature combination. Cell delay and leakage change substantially from one corner to the next, so a timing or power number carries no meaning unless the corner it was measured at travels with it.

The retained files record a five-event chronology. The preregistration was
frozen at 18:19:48 UTC. The response schema was rejected at 18:21:00 and amended
at 18:21:41. The valid model call ran from 18:21:51 to 18:22:24. The twelve
evaluations were recorded during one aggregate study-runner execution window
from 18:31:23 to 18:31:42. That window includes runner setup and result
serialization, not only simulator time. These internal timestamps record the
claimed order, but no external timestamp or commit binding independently proves
that order. The execution record also supplies only the aggregate window, not a
timestamp for each evaluation.

Three limits matter when interpreting this record. First, the valid proposal
used one call and no repair, so later candidate replacement cannot explain the
outcome. One call cannot establish the reliability or expected utility of a
model family. That program-level evaluation requires repeated model calls,
strong checks, and a design space capable of separating the compared methods;
@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect takes up that problem. Second, the requested
alias is not a pinned model identity, since a hosted model behind a fixed alias
can change [@ChenEtAl2024ChatGPTBehavior]. The response hash pins the retained
output rather than the hosted generator.

Third, the retained prompt copy does not match its recorded identity. Both the
preregistration and runtime provenance name SHA-256
`ec12df200a134532...76fbca`,
while the surviving `model_prompt.md` hashes to
`36e0167aa338c6b...6971`.
No matching prompt copy was found. The complete model response is retained,
but the package cannot verify the exact prompt that produced it. This mismatch
does not change the frozen simulator results or their replay, but it prevents
exact reconstruction of the generation context.

The protocol neither declared nor logged exploratory prompt iterations and
author hours before the freeze. A complete accounting would include that human
cost. The missing field is a limitation discovered after the run, not a frozen
requirement that the study satisfied.

### Interpreting Proposal Overlap

The model proposed 16 by 64, 8 by 128, and 32 by 16. The fixed aspect-ratio
heuristic ranked legal shapes by processing-element count, then by closeness to
the workload's aggregate N-to-M aspect ratio, with a deterministic tie break.
It proposed 16 by 64, 8 by 128, and 64 by 16. The two arms therefore selected
two of the same nonbaseline shapes. Including the shared 32 by 32 baseline, the
union contains five unique evaluated shapes from the fifteen legal shapes.

This overlap matters because the shared choices cannot be attributed uniquely
to the model. The arms agree on two of their three proposals and differ in only
one, where the model's 32 by 16 and the heuristic's 64 by 16 each rank worse.
With only fifteen legal shapes and a model compared against a weak fixed
heuristic that selected many of the same shapes, the comparison had little
resolving power[^fn-resolving-power-c08] to separate them. The result is a
numerical tie and a local non-demonstration of AI advantage, not evidence of
parity between the proposers.

[^fn-resolving-power-c08]: **Resolving power**: A design's ability to separate genuinely different candidates. The evaluation here is deterministic, so the immediate limit is discrimination rather than statistical power over evaluation noise. With few distinct legal shapes and substantial overlap between proposal sets, this comparison had little opportunity to show a difference.

## Results Under Matched Budgets

The validated candidate and workload identities became frozen SCALE-Sim input
configurations. The runner executed eight proposal-arm evaluations and four
shared mechanism probes. All twelve records report `status: ok`, and both the
processing-element and cycle checks pass in every record. The execution
provenance reports zero failures. Input and report hashes bind each evaluation
to its retained files. They do not repair the missing rejected-schema artifacts
or the prompt hash mismatch. Repeated shapes in different arms keep separate
evaluation identities, which preserves the declared arm budgets.

The matched simulator-call budget is only one part of the cost. The valid
model call took 32.90 seconds and used 13,223 input tokens, including 1,920
cached tokens, plus 1,446 output tokens, including 516 reasoning tokens. The
twelve evaluations were recorded inside a 19.05-second aggregate runner
window. Currency cost, queue time, per-evaluation runtime, compute, memory,
storage, license use, prompt-development effort, and total human effort were
not recorded. Equal simulator calls therefore support a narrow comparison of
proposal outcomes, not a claim of equal total cost.

Several legal alternatives ranked worse under the declared score, and no
nonbaseline shape cleared the decision margin across all eight arm evaluations
(@tbl-ai-study-results).

| **Arm** | **Shape and source** | **Cycles** | **Average layer utilization** | **Local score** | **Result within arm** |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Model | 32 by 32 baseline | 13,917 | 41.196% | 33,782.40 | Tied best |
| Model | 16 by 64 proposal | 13,917 | 41.196% | 33,782.40 | Tied best |
| Model | 8 by 128 proposal | 19,405 | 29.704% | 65,327.45 | Ranked worse |
| Model | 32 by 16 proposal | 25,277 | 45.438% | 55,629.61 | Ranked worse |
| Heuristic | 32 by 32 baseline | 13,917 | 41.196% | 33,782.40 | Tied best |
| Heuristic | 16 by 64 proposal | 13,917 | 41.196% | 33,782.40 | Tied best |
| Heuristic | 8 by 128 proposal | 19,405 | 29.704% | 65,327.45 | Ranked worse |
| Heuristic | 64 by 16 proposal | 17,757 | 32.294% | 54,985.25 | Ranked worse |

: **The model and fixed heuristic arms tie under equal simulator-call budgets.** Neither finds a nonbaseline candidate that clears the predeclared 1 percent decision margin over 32 by 32. Cycles and utilization come from SCALE-Sim; the retained runner computes the local score and recorded result. None of these values are measured on silicon. {#tbl-ai-study-results tbl-colwidths="[12,23,11,18,14,22]"}

Read the repeated baseline and 16-by-64 rows as separate arm-budget
evaluations, not as independent measurements. Within both arms, those two
shapes match exactly on cycles, utilization, and score. The 8-by-128 candidate
is worse on both cycles and utilization. The 32-by-16 model candidate shows why
utilization alone is insufficient: its higher utilization cannot offset its
substantially larger cycle count under the declared score. The table preserves
the exact values; the figure that follows makes their ranking and the separate
mechanism test easier to see.

Two panels keep the candidate comparison and mechanism test separate
(@fig-ai-study-result). The left asks whether either arm moves below the
baseline. The right asks whether the mirrored shapes exchange positions after
the workload transformation.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ai-study-result
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Results of the equal-simulator-call study and declared contrast.** The left panel reports every candidate score under equal four-run simulator budgets. The 32 by 32 baseline and 16 by 64 shape tie in both arms; lower is better. The right panel tests the model's directional prediction. The predicted winner reversal after transposing M and N does not occur. Cycles and utilization come from the retained SCALE-Sim 3.0.0 outputs; the retained runner computes scores and margins. None of the values are measured on silicon.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Two-panel study result. Horizontal bars show all model and fixed heuristic candidate scores, with the baseline and 16 by 64 tied at the lowest score in both arms. A paired-line plot shows 16 by 64 beating 64 by 16 on both the original and transposed workloads, contrary to the predicted reversal."

import json
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

result_path = Path("../labs/examples/ai_systolic_array_study/recorded/reference/study_results.json")
result = json.loads(result_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

arm_runs = [r for r in result["evaluations"] if r["arm"] in {"model", "conventional"}]
probe_runs = [r for r in result["evaluations"] if r["arm"] == "mechanism_probe"]

shape_labels = {
    "model_baseline_32x32": "M  32×32 baseline",
    "ai_wide_16x64": "M  16×64",
    "ai_extreme_8x128": "M  8×128",
    "ai_compact_32x16": "M  32×16",
    "conventional_baseline_32x32": "H  32×32 baseline",
    "heuristic_16x64": "H  16×64",
    "heuristic_8x128": "H  8×128",
    "heuristic_64x16": "H  64×16",
}

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(5.6, 2.65), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.35, 1]})
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.22, right=0.985, top=0.82, bottom=0.18, wspace=0.42)

labels = [shape_labels[r["candidate_id"]] for r in arm_runs]
scores = [r["decision_score"] / 1000 for r in arm_runs]
colors = [COLORS["blue"] if r["arm"] == "model" else COLORS["green"] for r in arm_runs]
y = list(range(len(arm_runs)))
ax1.barh(y, scores, color=colors, height=0.66)
ax1.set_yticks(y, labels)
ax1.invert_yaxis()

ax1.set_xlim(0, max(scores) * 1.18)

probe = {}
for run in probe_runs:
    workload = "transposed" if "transposed" in run["candidate_id"] else "original"
    shape = f'{run["array_rows"]}×{run["array_cols"]}'
    probe[(shape, workload)] = run["decision_score"] / 1000

x = [0, 1]
for shape, color, marker in [("16×64", COLORS["blue"], "o"), ("64×16", COLORS["orange"], "s")]:
    values = [probe[(shape, "original")], probe[(shape, "transposed")]]
    ax2.plot(x, values, marker=marker, markersize=4.2, linewidth=1.5, color=color, label=shape)
    for xi, value in zip(x, values):
        ax2.text(xi, value + 1.1, f"{value:.1f}", ha="center", fontsize=5.5, color=color)

ax2.set_xticks(x, ["original", "M/N transposed"])
ax2.set_ylabel("local score (thousands)", fontsize=6.5)
ax2.set_title("Mechanism probe: no reversal", fontsize=7, pad=5)
ax2.set_ylim(18, 61)
ax2.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=6, loc="upper right")

for ax in (ax1, ax2):
    ax.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=5.9, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
    ax.grid(axis="x" if ax is ax1 else "y", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.55, zorder=0)

    ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
```
