In the left panel, the 32 by 32 baseline and 16 by 64 candidate have the same
shortest bar in both arms. No nonbaseline shape moves below the baseline. In the
right panel, 16 by 64 remains below 64 by 16 after M and N are exchanged. The
gap narrows, but the lines do not cross.

The first panel shows why no change is
warranted for the five evaluated shapes and why the two proposal arms tie on
the local score derived by the retained runner from simulator outputs. It does
not establish that 32 by 32 is optimal across all fifteen legal shapes or that
the two methods consumed equal total effort. The right panel probes the
mechanism behind these proposals, which requires a dedicated contrast test.

## Test the Explanation and Escalate

As shown in the right panel of @fig-ai-study-result, the model predicted that 16 by 64 would beat its mirrored 64 by 16 shape on the
original workload because the wider array would align better with the supplied
N dimensions. It also predicted that exchanging M and N would reverse the
winner. This is a testable prediction because it names a direction and a
failure condition.

Each margin below compares the two shapes on one workload, so the four runs form two within-workload pairs rather than a single cross-workload comparison. On the original workload, 16 by 64 wins by 38.56 percent, with scores of
33,782.40 and 54,985.25. After transposition, it still wins by 7.57 percent,
23,530.65 to 25,458.11. The predicted reversal does not occur. The margin does narrow sharply, evidence that the transposition changed something the failed explanation cannot account for, even though the shift stopped short of a reversal.

The directional prediction therefore fails its declared contrast. The
surviving prompt copy did not pin the mapping semantics, and the package cannot
establish whether the recorded call did. Independently, the contrast did not
isolate orientation. The result therefore neither shows that orientation is
irrelevant nor supplies a replacement explanation.

The mapping-semantic gap in the surviving prompt copy became clear only after
the run. Under SCALE-Sim's weight-stationary GEMM mode, the resident weight
tile is K by N. Array height carries K, array width carries N, and M streams
through the array (@fig-array-mapping). The model's assumption that width
tracks N was conventional, but the retained package cannot establish what
binding the recorded call received or whether the model reasoned from it.

![**The axis binding omitted from the surviving prompt copy.** Under SCALE-Sim's weight-stationary GEMM mode, array height carries K and array width carries N, while M streams through the array. Exchanging M and N leaves K unchanged, so the mirrored shapes move more than one fold count. The contrast tests the recorded directional prediction but does not isolate orientation as a cause.](images/F8-array-mapping){#fig-array-mapping fig-alt="A GEMM workload feeds a resident weight tile of K by N, which maps onto wide 16 by 64 and tall 64 by 16 arrays. K maps over array height and N over array width. A dashed transpose connector notes that K is unchanged, so the mirrored pair changes more than one fold count."}

The transposition still tests the model's exact directional prediction, but it
is not a causally isolated test of orientation. Exchanging M and N leaves K
untouched, while mirroring 16 by 64 and 64 by 16 changes both the N-fold count
on the width axis and the K-fold count on the height axis. The test therefore
probes the prompt's completeness and the contrast design as well as the
model's architectural reasoning. A stronger follow-up must pin the mapping
semantics in the prompt and vary one fold count at a time.

### Judging the Four Claims

With the candidate evaluations and the mechanism contrast complete, the
architect can now resolve the four distinct judgments fixed in the predeclared
study plan. The four conclusions in @tbl-study-claim-dispositions answer
distinctly different questions.

| **Claim** | **Observed evidence** | **Conclusion** | **Outside this conclusion** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Architecture outcome** | Best evaluated nonbaseline ties the baseline; improvement is 0.0%. | No change under the 1 percent decision margin for the five evaluated shapes. | No claim about the ten unevaluated legal shapes, another workload, or another objective. |
| **AI contribution** | Best scores tie at four simulator calls per arm; two nonbaseline selections overlap. | No study-local AI advantage is demonstrated against the weak fixed heuristic. | Total effort is unknown, and no broader claim about a model family follows. |
| **Mechanism explanation** | 16 by 64 wins on both workloads. | The directional prediction fails its declared contrast. | No causally isolated replacement explanation, especially without pinned mapping semantics. |
| **Stopping decision** | No selected candidate clears the decision margin, and post-result replacement is prohibited. | Stop the local search and recommend retaining 32 by 32 for the evaluated set. | The architecture action remains pending; 32 by 32 is not claimed optimal among all fifteen legal shapes. |

: **The four judgments have different conclusions.** The architecture outcome, AI contribution, mechanism explanation, and stopping decision remain separate. {#tbl-study-claim-dispositions tbl-colwidths="[19,31,18,32]"}

The first row asks whether any new shape warrants a change under the local
score. The second asks whether the model found an advantage over the heuristic
under the same simulator-call budget. The third tests only the model's
explanation. The fourth records what the architect does next. Each conclusion
follows from different evidence.

A different run could split them. A candidate that cleared the margin would set the architecture outcome to a change and still leave the stopping decision at stop, if the evaluation budget were spent or the gain did not justify the cost of verifying it. In this run no candidate cleared the margin, so the outcome and the stopping decision point the same way, and the mechanism verdict stands apart from both.

The frozen protocol permits no post-result replacement, and no candidate
clears the decision margin, so the technical study stops here. Its
recommendation is to retain 32 by 32 for the five evaluated shapes because a
nonbaseline tie does not justify change under the declared rule. The
architecture action remains pending. A broader workload, another dataflow,
pinned mapping semantics, a calibrated memory model, or implementation-adjacent
constraints would require a new study rather than an extension of this run.

## Return to XR and Stop Honestly

The local result now has to be put back into the system question that motivated
it. For the synthetic workloads, the retained score gives no reason to replace
32 by 32 with one of the four evaluated nonbaseline shapes. That finding does
not show that the array meets an XR deadline, that its software stack can keep
it busy, or that the complete subsystem fits within 3\ W.

The workload mapping, compiler and runtime path, shared-memory behavior,
precision choice, verification plan, energy and thermal behavior, host
interfaces, and physical implementation therefore remain unresolved. So do
the ten legal array shapes that the frozen run did not evaluate. An exhaustive
enumeration, a solver-based comparison, or an expert-designed diagnostic would
be required before making a broader claim about candidate-selection methods.
None was run here, and none can be added after the fact to strengthen this
record.

The local technical disposition and the system commitment must remain
separate. The study stops with a recommendation to retain 32 by 32 for the
evaluated set. No architecture change has been authorized, and the record
names no accountable owner. The Lighthouse system remains an open design
problem.

One completed record keeps the frozen plan, its four judgments, and the
pending architecture action together (@tbl-practitioner-path).

| **Record field** | **Completed local record** |
| --- | --- |
| **Frozen plan** | Three-layer GEMM slice, 32 by 32 baseline, fifteen legal shapes, fixed simulator configuration, local score, 1 percent margin, four calls per proposal arm, and four shared mechanism probes. |
| **Execution** | One pre-inference schema rejection, one schema-valid model response, eight proposal-arm evaluations, four mechanism probes, and five unique evaluated shapes. The retained record supplies call counts and a 19.05-second aggregate runner window, but not per-attempt queue time, run time, compute, memory, storage, or license use. Total human effort remains unknown. |
| **Measurements** | SCALE-Sim cycles, utilization, and modeled memory traffic under the retained inputs and version. No silicon, timing-closure, physical-design, or measured-energy result. |
| **Architecture outcome** | No evaluated nonbaseline shape clears the declared margin. This is a no-change study outcome for the five evaluated shapes, not an optimality result. |
| **Study-local AI contribution** | The model arm and weak fixed heuristic tie on the frozen score under equal simulator-call budgets. The comparison demonstrates no local AI advantage and does not measure total effort or model reliability. |
| **Mechanism status** | The predicted winner reversal does not occur. The directional explanation fails. A replacement mechanism remains unresolved because the surviving prompt copy omitted mapping semantics, the exact recorded context cannot be verified, and the contrast did not isolate orientation. |
| **Stopping and decision status** | The local technical study stops. Retaining 32 by 32 is the recorded recommendation, no architecture change has been authorized, and the record does not name the accountable owner. |
| **Record limits** | The exact model prompt cannot be verified because the retained copy does not match the recorded hash. The rejection checks did not fire inside the study, the score omitted modeled memory traffic, and replay shares the study's simulator, workload, score, and assumptions. |
| **Reopening conditions** | Reopen through a newly frozen study if the workload, objective, dataflow, mapping semantics, simulator, model identity, energy model, implementation constraints, or decision scope changes, or if an independent check contradicts the recorded result. |

: **The completed local record separates outcome from action.** The study is
technically closed, its recommendation is explicit, and the architecture action
remains pending.
{#tbl-practitioner-path tbl-colwidths="[24,66]"}

Read down from the frozen plan through execution and measurements before
reaching the architecture-outcome, AI-contribution, mechanism, and stopping
fields. The final rows state the record limits and the conditions that require
a new study. This order keeps the conclusions attached to what actually ran
and what the tools returned. It also preserves the difference between a
technically closed study and an architecture action that still lacks
confirmation and a named owner. Assigning that owner later would create a
dated post-study action record; it would not rewrite the preregistered roles or
the historical run.

### Auditing the Study After Closure

The frozen outcome and four judgments are already closed. The observations in
this section were made by examining the completed record and therefore audit
the study design rather than extend its chronology. They can motivate a new
study, but they cannot add a metric, replace the comparator, or rescore this
run.

Every proposed candidate passed the processing-element and cycle-limit checks,
so this run demonstrates its three declared control checks only in the passing
direction. It does not exercise the invalid-candidate repair path, the
illegal-shape rejection, or the 90,000-cycle cutoff. A future confirmatory run
can include a positive control, such as a shape that violates the
processing-element budget or a run known to cross the cycle cutoff, and require
the harness to reject it before the proposal arms are scored. Such a control
tests the rejection path without converting the invalid candidate into part of
either arm.

The 16 by 64 candidate exactly matches the baseline's cycles, average layer
utilization, and local score. The exact tie is not a consequence of equal
resources alone, since the 8 by 128 shape also has 1,024 processing elements
yet takes 39 percent more cycles. The layers fold onto 32 by 32 and 16 by 64
in the same number of tiles with no edge waste. In SCALE-Sim's closed form for
this mode, $M + 2h + w - 2$, the shape-dependent pipeline term $2h + w - 2$ is
94 for both. Equal tile counts alone do not produce the tie. The heuristic's
64 by 16 shape folds into the same eighty tiles at full mapping efficiency and
still takes 27.6 percent more cycles.

That arithmetic exposes a weakness in the study design. Under this frozen
dataflow, a paper analysis of fold counts, edge waste, and pipeline cost could
have ranked the cycle behavior of the fifteen legal shapes before simulation.
The simulator calls still provide the evidence used by the frozen protocol,
but a preliminary analytical pass could have avoided spending evaluations on
differences already predicted in closed form. The ten unexecuted shapes remain
outside the reported outcome because the protocol required simulator results,
not paper predictions.

The tie also hides a difference that the frozen score does not use.[^fn-dram-traffic]
The 16 by 64 shape has the same cycles and utilization as the baseline but
twice its modeled DRAM-word writes. On the two simulator-reported axes of
cycles and modeled word writes, the baseline dominates that shared candidate
(@fig-proxy-mismatch). The observation does not change the frozen score or
outcome. It reveals that the score omitted a decision-relevant axis. The
blindness runs both ways. The heuristic's 64 by 16 shape has half the
baseline's modeled word writes and 31 percent fewer total modeled DRAM-word
accesses,
while taking 27.6 percent more cycles. A later energy-aware study could value
that tradeoff differently [@Horowitz2014Energy].

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="The omitted memory axis in the 3\ W XR system"}
The modeled write ratio raises a system question rather than answering one.
In the Lighthouse interpretation, an accelerator serving spatial tracking
would share its memory path with the RISC-V host cores and XR display engine,
so extra traffic could consume bandwidth and energy needed elsewhere. The
synthetic workload does not establish that such traffic occurs in the
Lighthouse system, and this study measures neither contention nor physical energy.
SCALE-Sim reports one-byte interface words in this configuration, not
identified DRAM transactions, so converting the counts into energy requires a
memory-system model that this run does not have.
:::

An architect who discovered this proxy mismatch after a run
(@sec-feedback-verification-trust) would not rescore the completed results
against a new objective. A new preregistration could replace the
cycles-and-utilization score with one that prices data movement, such as an
energy-delay product $\text{EDP} = E_{\text{total}} \times \text{cycles}$,
where an architecture-level energy model estimates compute, SRAM, and DRAM
energy [@WuEtAl2019Accelergy]. That would be a new confirmatory study rather
than a rescoring of this one. No such amendment was filed here. This study
reports the tie under the score it froze, and the memory axis remains a stated
limitation.

```{python}
#| label: fig-proxy-mismatch
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **The frozen score omits modeled memory traffic.** The local score ranks the shared 16 by 64 candidate exactly equal to the 32 by 32 baseline. Across two SCALE-Sim outputs, cycles and modeled DRAM-word writes, the baseline dominates that candidate. This post-run observation does not change the frozen outcome; it motivates a new score and study.
#| out-width: "80%"
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of evaluated systolic array shapes using two SCALE-Sim outputs. The 32 by 32 baseline and shared 16 by 64 candidate both take 13,917 cycles, while the shared candidate reports about twice the modeled DRAM-word writes."

import json
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

result_path = Path("../labs/examples/ai_systolic_array_study/recorded/reference/study_results.json")
result = json.loads(result_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

# We will just plot all evaluated runs
arm_runs = [r for r in result["evaluations"] if r["arm"] in {"model", "conventional"}]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 3.5))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.18, right=0.95, top=0.88, bottom=0.15)

ax.set_title("Frozen Score Omits Modeled Memory Traffic", fontsize=7.5, pad=8)
ax.set_xlabel("Compute Cycles (lower is better)", fontsize=6.5)
ax.set_ylabel("Modeled DRAM-word writes (lower is better)", fontsize=6.5)

# Deduplicate points by candidate_id
seen = set()
for r in arm_runs:
    cid = r["candidate_id"]
    if cid in seen: continue
    seen.add(cid)

    cycles = r["gates"]["deadline"]["observed"]
    dram_writes = r["metrics"]["dram_writes"]

    label = cid.replace("model_baseline_", "").replace("ai_wide_", "").replace("ai_extreme_", "").replace("ai_compact_", "").replace("conventional_baseline_", "").replace("heuristic_", "")

    if "32x32" in label:
        color = COLORS["blue"]
        marker = "o"
        label_text = f"Baseline\n{label}"
        ax.plot(cycles, dram_writes, marker=marker, markersize=5, color=color)
        ax.text(cycles - 500, dram_writes - 10000, label_text, color=COLORS["ink"], fontsize=5.5, ha="right", va="top")
    elif "16x64" in label:
        color = COLORS["red"]
        marker = "X"
        label_text = f"Shared candidate\n{label}"
        ax.plot(cycles, dram_writes, marker=marker, markersize=5, color=color)
        ax.text(cycles + 300, dram_writes + 15000, label_text, color=COLORS["ink"], fontsize=5.5, ha="left", va="bottom")
    else:
        color = COLORS["orange"]
        marker = "s"
        ax.plot(cycles, dram_writes, marker=marker, markersize=4, color=color, alpha=0.6)
        ax.text(cycles + 300, dram_writes, label, color=COLORS["ink"], fontsize=5, ha="left", va="center", alpha=0.7)

# Mark the shared minimum-cycle coordinate
ax.axvline(x=13917, color=COLORS["grid"], linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8, zorder=0)

ax.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=5.9, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
ax.grid(True, color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.55, zorder=0)
for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])

plt.show()
```

[^fn-dram-traffic]: At identical cycles and utilization, SCALE-Sim reports 409,726 one-byte DRAM-word writes for 16 by 64 against 204,863 for the baseline, twice as many, and about 1.6 times the total modeled word accesses.

Read toward the lower-left because both axes are lower-is-better simulator
outputs. The baseline and shared 16 by 64 candidate align at 13,917 cycles, but
the shared candidate sits much higher on modeled DRAM-word writes. The baseline
therefore dominates that candidate on these two reported quantities even
though the frozen composite score ties them. The plot exposes an omitted axis;
it does not authorize post-run rescoring or establish physical memory energy.

The 16 by 64 candidate already fails to advance under the frozen rule because
it does not clear the one-percent margin. The post-run modeled-write
observation supplies no reason to override that stop and motivates a new
memory-aware study. It does not rescore this run or establish that 16 by 64 is
physically or energetically inferior.

The 32 by 16 shape has higher average layer utilization than the baseline but
takes far more cycles, so the composite rule ranks it worse. The 8 by 128 shape
loses on both ingredients. A reader who disagrees with the composite score can
still inspect those raw quantities and challenge the rule without rerunning
the study.

An elongated 8 by 128 or 16 by 64 block might also cost more in wire length,
Network-on-Chip (NoC) routing congestion, timing closure, and global
interconnect power than a compact 32 by 32 block. That is a reasonable
hypothesis, but it is not a result of this run. SCALE-Sim performs no timing
closure or physical design, and this run enabled no energy model. Testing the
hypothesis would require a new tier of tooling, such as a floorplan or
place-and-route estimate.

Before a confirmatory run, the evaluator should test whether the proposed
comparison can distinguish the arms. A pilot or analytical pass can estimate
proposal overlap and score sensitivity. The actual comparison should then run
on workloads or cases that were not used to tune the proposal rules, prompt,
heuristic, or score. Evaluator-owned positive controls should exercise the
legality and cutoff paths without entering either proposal arm. The exact
prompt, schema, tool configuration, and preregistration should be bound to the
record before inference. Prompt development, comparator tuning, and score
selection belong to the development phase; confirmation begins only after
those choices are frozen. These changes define a new study. They do not
retroactively strengthen this one.

### Packaging the Study {#sec-ai-study-archive}

The retained package contains the preregistration, complete model response,
recorded provenance, exact simulator inputs, raw summary reports, parsed
results, hashes, tests, and replay code. The prompt-hash mismatch prevents it
from carrying the exact generation context, but the simulator record remains
intact. The study contains no proprietary PDK data or RTL, so no protected
design data required redaction. A production package would also need to protect
confidential inputs. The files are versioned with the repository, although the
package manifest does not itself record a commit identity. The historical
execution record still contains a local executable path, so the package is not
fully path-scrubbed or self-contained.

The preregistration carries the fixed heuristic rule and declared candidates.
The executable heuristic implementation lives in repository code, but the
manifest does not bind that code to a commit. A reviewer can inspect the
declaration and retained outputs without treating the manifest as proof of the
exact historical implementation.

The [companion README](https://github.com/harvard-edge/arch2/blob/main/labs/examples/ai_systolic_array_study/README.md)
lists the retained files, replay commands, and known provenance limits.

#### Mapping Artifacts to Review Questions

Each retained artifact answers a specific review question
(@tbl-study-archive).

| **Artifact** | **What it lets a reviewer check** |
| --- | --- |
| **Preregistration** | The recorded chronology declaring claims, candidates per arm, rejection criteria, score, decision margin, repair limit, contrast, and decision boundary before inference and simulation. Without an external timestamp or commit binding, the file does not independently prove precedence. |
| **Model prompt, schema, and full response** | Whether the printed proposals and prediction match the retained response. The prompt copy shows the intended context but cannot establish the exact context because its hash does not match the frozen record. |
| **Provenance record** | Requested model alias, interface, timestamps, exposed settings, usage, response hash, pre-inference error, and unavailable identity fields. |
| **Fixed aspect-ratio heuristic** | The preregistration records the rule and declared candidates. The executable implementation is in repository code, but the manifest does not bind it to a commit, so the exact historical code identity is not established by the package alone. |
| **Reference evaluations and execution provenance** | Exact topology, layout, SCALE-Sim configuration, raw run locations, parsed metrics, rejection results, and conclusions for all twelve evaluations. |
| **Reference manifest and replay** | Whether retained files match their hashes and a network-free rerun regenerates every stable input, report, metric, and result. |

: **Each review question maps to a retained artifact.** These files do not establish that the simulator is accurate or the workload representative, and the prompt mismatch leaves one provenance question unresolved. {#tbl-study-archive tbl-colwidths="[26,64]"}

Read from the declaration artifacts to the model and provenance files, then to
the fixed heuristic, raw evaluations, manifest, and replay. The first group
lets a reviewer inspect what was intended and what the model returned. The
second connects those declarations to the executed simulator results and
retained hashes. Together they support review and replay of the recorded
computation, but they do not establish simulator fidelity or workload
representativeness.

#### What Each Follow-up Checks

The package supports different follow-up actions that answer different
questions (@tbl-verification-levels). They do not form an automatic hierarchy
in which one result proves the next.

| **Follow-up** | **Study status** | **What a successful result would support** | **What it would not establish** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Reference integrity check** | The retained manifest can be checked against the archived files. | The archived files still match their recorded hashes and sizes. | That the computation can be regenerated or that the simulator is faithful. |
| **Deterministic simulator replay** | A network-free replay path is packaged; completion must be reported separately. | The retained runner, simulator version, inputs, and parsing regenerate the stable study outputs. | Simulator fidelity, workload representativeness, or an independent result. |
| **Generator re-execution** | Exact reproduction is unavailable because provider revision and seed were not exposed and the retained prompt hash does not match. | A new call could measure behavior of the currently available model and runtime. | Recreation of the recorded proposal or truth of the architecture claim. |
| **Independent architecture check** | Not performed. | A different implementation or testbench could test whether the local result or proposed mechanism survives different modeling assumptions. | Automatic removal of every shared specification, workload, or modeling error. |

: **Each follow-up answers a different question.** Replay tests computational
repeatability under shared assumptions; a separately designed check can reduce
some shared assumptions without becoming ground truth. {#tbl-verification-levels tbl-colwidths="[20,22,30,28]"}

Read downward as four different questions rather than four levels of proof.
Reference integrity asks whether the retained files changed. Simulator replay
asks whether the same computation can be regenerated. Generator re-execution
tests current behavior without recreating the recorded call, while an
independent architecture check changes part of the modeling path. Success in
one row cannot supply the conclusion reserved for another.

#### Verifying the Replay

The preregistration records what was declared before inference. The model
artifacts retain the response while exposing the prompt-identity gap. The raw
reports and parsed results show what SCALE-Sim returned, and the manifest and
replay code connect the reported numbers back to retained files. Together,
those records let another architect check the declared simulator computation
without implying that SCALE-Sim is accurate enough for a different claim or
that the workload represents the full system intent.

Offline replay needs no network account or model credential. It verifies the
reference, reruns all twelve evaluations, and compares their stable inputs,
summary reports, metrics, and hashes. Large deterministic access traces are
regenerated rather than archived. That choice assumes the pinned simulator
version and configuration regenerate the traces used for the reported
metrics. The package compares stable summary reports and parsed results; any
disagreement requires investigation rather than a presumption about which
artifact is correct.

An optional provider-neutral live adapter writes to a separate output directory
and checks the requested model alias. That check does not recover the exact
provider revision or digest used for the recorded call. The adapter halts if the
runtime or credential is unavailable, the response is invalid, or a proposed
geometry is illegal. It never changes the recorded reference results. Commands
and failure details remain in the companion rather than the printed chapter.

A successful replay confirms that the retained computation can be regenerated
under the retained code and inputs in a compatible environment matching the
documented versions. It is not an independent
result because it shares the same runner, simulator, workload, score, and
assumptions. It does not validate SCALE-Sim against fabricated silicon,
establish workload representativeness, justify the local score or thresholds,
resolve the missing mapping semantics, or predict another model call. Those
are new claims requiring new evidence.

## Open Research Questions

The local result exposes research problems that recur whenever a system goal
is reduced to a tool-evaluable decision.

### System-to-Local Decomposition

**How should a full-system requirement be decomposed without losing its causal
link to the local decision?** The local objective must remain traceable to the
system outcome it is meant to improve, even when the full system cannot yet be
executed.

**When are synthetic stand-ins representative enough to guide a design
decision?** A useful answer needs tests for missing workload phases, software
effects, resource contention, and operating conditions rather than a claim of
similarity based only on kernel type.

**How should mapping semantics be represented before a mechanism is tested?**
A dataflow name alone does not bind workload dimensions to array dimensions,
and an omitted binding can make a contrast test the prompt rather than the
mechanism.

### Comparison and Run Design

**How should generative, heuristic, solver-based, and expert proposal methods
be compared when candidates overlap and feedback costs differ?** Equal tool
calls control one resource, but they do not equalize prior knowledge, model
inference, setup effort, or human time.

**How should an energy-relevant axis enter a selection score, and what would
make the underlying architecture energy model adequate?** A sensitivity
calculation can expose a missing axis without establishing that an unvalidated
energy estimate is reliable enough to guide candidate selection.

**How should proposal quality and explanation quality be evaluated
separately?** A useful candidate may arrive with a false explanation, while a
failed candidate can still state a mechanism worth testing in another
comparison.

**How can a study assess its resolving power and exercise its rejection paths
before execution?** A small candidate space and overlapping proposal rules can
make a tie likely even when the proposers differ. Evaluator-owned positive
controls can test safety checks without entering invalid candidates into the
architecture comparison.

**Which candidates should be screened analytically before simulation?** A
simple model can reserve expensive tool calls for questions that arithmetic
cannot settle.

### Escalation and System Return

**What independent check best challenges a simulator result?** A different
implementation can reduce shared tool assumptions while still sharing the
same specification, workload, or blind spot.

**How should a local result be returned to a system decision?** The record
needs explicit rules for what transfers, what remains unresolved, who can
approve a change, and what evidence requires a new study.

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Return every local result to the system question"}
Close the architecture outcome, AI contribution, mechanism explanation, and
stopping decision separately. Then state what the local result does and does
not establish about the system that motivated it. Finishing a local study does
not authorize a system change.
:::

The study began with a 3\ W XR system goal and reduced it to one array-shape
decision over three synthetic GEMMs. The four judgments are clear. None of the
four evaluated nonbaseline shapes clears the 1 percent decision margin over 32
by 32. The model arm shows no local advantage over the fixed heuristic
under four simulator calls per arm. The model's directional explanation fails
its declared contrast. The technical study stops rather than replacing a
candidate or score after seeing the result.

The 16 by 64 candidate does not advance because it fails to clear the frozen
one-percent margin. A post-run audit also finds that it reports more modeled
writes than the baseline, but that observation does not rescore the study or
establish physical or energy inferiority. The score omitted memory traffic,
the simulator supplied no timing, area, power, thermal, or physical result,
and the synthetic GEMMs were not taken from an identified XR pipeline.

The retained history also remains imperfect. The exact prompt cannot be
verified, the manifest does not bind the heuristic implementation to a commit,
total effort is unknown, and replay shares the original workload, simulator,
score, and assumptions. No exhaustive enumeration, solver-based comparison,
expert diagnostic, or independent architecture check was performed. The study
therefore supports neither array optimality nor a broad claim about AI-assisted
candidate selection.

The local recommendation is to retain 32 by 32 for the evaluated set. The
architecture action remains pending, with no named owner, and the XR system
commitment remains open. Its workload fidelity,
software path, shared-memory behavior, verification, 3\ W budget, thermal
behavior, and physical implementation still require their own decisions and
measurements.
